claims.text: The proposed framework will calculate lattice and electronic heat transport separately.
The framework will predict lattice thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr within ±20% of experiment from 300 to 1200 K.
HfNbTaTiZr exhibits a distinct low-temperature thermal-conductivity plateau below 200 K.
The relevant initial material is single-phase, polycrystalline bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
Keeping oxygen at approximately 1 wt.% or less minimizes extrinsic scattering beyond intrinsic alloy disorder.
The lattice model will combine DFT-derived phonon dispersions with a Boltzmann transport formulation that includes point-defect and oxygen-impurity scattering.
Electronic thermal conductivity will be calculated independently using electronic-structure and electron-phonon-coupling estimates.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
Reported high-temperature measurements from 300 to 1200 K concern a HfNbTaTiZr specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Mass fluctuations, force-constant variations, point defects, and oxygen impurities scatter phonons in HfNbTaTiZr.
Treating phonon-scattering mechanisms separately from electronic transport permits accurate attribution of each heat-conduction channel.
Decoupling lattice and electronic transport avoids errors caused by conflating the two contributions.
A refined DFT-Boltzmann treatment captures phonon dispersion and defect-induced scattering more accurately than earlier approaches.
Earlier approaches used global Debye-temperature approximations and conflated lattice and electronic transport.
Earlier approaches typically produced errors of approximately 50% or more relative to experiment.
Below 200 K, the calculation will reproduce the experimentally observed balance between phonon and electronic contributions.
At high temperature, the predicted lattice contribution will agree within ±20% with an experimentally isolated lattice contribution.
The approach is expected to be reliable for bulk samples containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen or less from about 100 to 1200 K.
Outside the stated temperature range, extreme defect scattering or high-temperature phase instability may require model extensions.
Grain-boundary scattering is not explicitly included even though the proposed material is polycrystalline.
